I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Petroleum & Natural Gas, having 
been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on their behalf, present this 
Seventh Report on ‘Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas’. 
 
2. The Committee examined the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Ministry of 
Petroleum & Natural Gas for the year 2026-27 which were laid on the Table of the 
House on 10.02.2026.

adopted by the Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas on 12.03.2026.  
 
4. The Committee wish to express their thanks to the representatives of the Ministry 
of Petroleum and Natural Gas for furnishing the material and information in connection 
with the examination of Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Ministry and for giving

PART I 
Introductory                     
India’s petroleum, and natural gas industry stands as the backbone of its energy 
sector, fueling the country’s rapid economic growth and urbanization. As the third-
largest consumer of energy in the world, India’s requirement for hydrocarbons continues 
to surge. Its total primary energy demand is expected to almost double, increasing from 
around 22 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2024 to about 43.6 million barrels 
of oil equivalent per day by 2050.  As per International Energy Agency (IEA), India will 
contribute over 40% of the global increase in oil demand and about 8% of the growth in 
natural gas demand between 2024 and 2025.  
 As the country’s energy demand rises faster than that of any other major 
economy, guaranteeing secure, affordable and reliable oil and gas supplies is vital. 
However, India’s energy journey is unfolding at a time of unprecedented flux in global 
markets where geopolitical tensions, supply disruptions and climate imperatives coexist 
and interact in complex ways.   
The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, at the helm of policy formulation and 
sectoral oversight, has introduced various transformative initiatives to boost investment, 
enhance domestic production and promote equitable access to clean fuels.  As per the 
Ministry, India holds proven oil reserves of around 4.5 billion barrels and natural gas 
reserves of nearly 1.3 trillion cubic meters. Despite these resources, the nation remains 
reliant on imports for over 85% of its crude oil needs, underscoring the imperative for 
both increased domestic exploration and strategic diversification of supply sources. 
 Against this backdrop, the allocation for the Ministry during the financial year 
2026-27 has been examined in the Report. The Ministry presented their Demands for 
Grants presented to the Parliament on 10th February, 2026 under Demand No. 76.

IV. Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG (DBTL) 
1.10 DBTL - Pahal Scheme was launched on 15th November 2014 with the approval of 
Cabinet vide note dated 18.10.2014, initially in 54 districts and subsequently extended 
to 622 districts from 01.01.2015. This initiative of the Government was aimed at 
rationalizing subsidies based on an approach to cut subsidy leakages, but not subsidies 
per se. As on 01.01.2026 PSU OMCs (IOCL, BPCL and HPCL) together have 33.21 
crore active LPG customers in the domestic category who are being served by 25,481 
LPG distributors. PSU OMCs enrolled 112.5 lakh new domestic customers in FY 2023-
24. More than 30.61 Crore LPG consumers have joined the Scheme as on 01.01.2026.  
 
1.11 When the Committee desired to know about the extant subsidy on Petrol, LPG 
and Kerosene and details of the subsidy being provided presently per cylinder of LPG 
and per litre of PDS Kerosene, the Ministry submitted the following information:        
“Petrol: Prices of petrol and diesel are market determined and Public Sector Oil 
Marketing Companies (OMCs) take appropriate decision on pricing of petrol and 
diesel in line with their international product prices, exchange rate, tax structure, 
inland freight and other cost elements. Hence there is NO Government of India 
subsidy on petrol. 
 
LPG: In order to insulate the common man from the impact of rise in international 
oil prices, the Government continues to modulate the effective price to consumer 
of Domestic LPG.   
 
The retail selling price of a 14.2 Kg domestic LPG cylinder is currently Rs 853 in 
Delhi. After a targeted subsidy of Rs 300/cylinder to PMUY consumers, 
Government of India is providing 14.2 Kg LPG cylinders at an effective price of 
Rs.553 per cylinder (in Delhi). This is available to all Ujjwala beneficiaries, across 
the country.

and the significant underspending.  In this regard, the Ministry furnished the following

V. LPG Connection to Poor Household (Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana)  
1.16 Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) was launched in May, 2016 with an 
objective to provide deposit free LPG connection to adult women from poor households 
across the country. The target to release 8 crore connections under PMUY was 
achieved in September 2019. To cover the remaining poor households, Ujjwala 2.0 was 
launched in August 2021 with a target to release 1 crore additional PMUY connections, 
which was achieved in January 2022. Subsequently, the Government decided to 
release 60 lakh more LPG connections under Ujjwala 2.0 and the target of 1.60 crore 
Ujjwala 2.0 connections was also achieved during December 2022. Further, 
Government approved release of additional 75 lakh connections under PMUY Scheme 
for the period FY 2023-24 to 2025-26 which has already been achieved during July 
2024. Government has recently approved the release of 25 lakh additional LPG 
connections under PMUY during Financial Year 2025-26 to achieve saturation of LPG 
access in the country. To further improve access, the eligibility criteria have been 
simplified to “Adult women from poor households based on submission of a Deprivation 
declaration”. As on 01.01.2026, there were 10.43 crore PMUY connections across the 
country.  

10 
 
1.17 On being asked about the number of connections that have been released to 
households under this scheme during the current financial year vis-a-vis the target for 
FY 2026-27, the Ministry submitted the following information:  
  
“PMUY Scheme was initiated in May, 2016 and as on 01.01.2026, a total no. 
of 10.43 Crore connections have been released. For the current financial year 
2025-26, Government approved the release of 25 lakhs additional connections 
under PMUY in Sep, 2025, out of which OMCs have released 10.35 lakh 
connections as on 01.01.2026.”

1.18 On being asked about the total PMUY provision of Rs.9,200 crore for 2026-27 
being split into three separate heads [viz., 'New LPG Connection under PMUY', 
'Targeted subsidy Payment to PMUY, (iii) PME/IEC Campaign Expenses under PMUY], 
following EFC (Expenditure Finance Committee) recommendations and the details 
regarding the same, the Ministry submitted written information as under:  
 
“It is submitted that all type of expenditure related to implementation of PMUY 
Scheme i.e. reimbursement of the claim for PMUY New connections, 
reimbursement of Targeted subsidy to PMUY beneficiaries and expenses related 
to PME/IEC campaign were being booked under the single head of LPG 
Connection to Poor Households.  
In order to streamline the budgeting & accounting related to different types of 
expenditure under the scheme, three separate heads have now been opened 
and will be operational from the next financial year. The action is in compliance of 
the recommendations received in the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) 
meeting held for appraisal of “Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY)” for FY 
2025–26 wherein the EFC had recommended that separate budget lines be 
maintained for (a) deposit-free connections under PMUY, (b) targeted subsidy to 
PMUY beneficiaries, and (c) PME/IEC/administrative charges.

VI. One-Time Grant to PSU OMCs for Under Recoveries in Domestic LPG 
 
1.22 With regard to one-time grant to PSU OMCs, the Ministry has submitted that 
during the period 2020-21 to 2022-23, as the increase in international LPG prices was 
not fully passed on in retail prices, the Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) suffered 
significant losses on domestic LPG. To compensate the OMCs for these losses, 
Government paid a one-time compensation of Rs. 22,000 crore to OMCs in January 
2023. The international prices of LPG again went up during 2024-25 and continue to 
remain high. However, to insulate consumers from fluctuations in international LPG 
prices, the increase in cost was not passed on to consumers of domestic LPG which led 

13 
 
to significant losses for the three OMCs. To compensate the OMCs for these losses, 
Government has recently approved a compensation of Rs. 30,000 crore to the OMCs. 
1.23 Having observed that the Government gave a one-time grant of Rs. 22,000 crore 
in January 2023 for LPG losses in 2020-21 to 2022-23 and has also recently approved 
another Rs. 30,000 crore as compensation for high international LPG prices in 2024-25, 
over and above the normal subsidy, the Committee wished to know how the losses of 
OMCs are calculated so that the same loss is not counted twice and they are not over-
compensated. In this regard, the Ministry furnished the following reply:  
“Computation of the under recoveries/losses faced by OMCs and corresponding 
compensation do not involve double counting. Since all bills raised by the OMCs 
are duly checked and vetted by the Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell (PPAC). 
Further, the Ministry, through its Integrated Finance Division, ensures robust 
checking before approving sanction of expenditure. 
Other subsidies like targeted subsidy to PMUY consumers of ₹200/- or ₹300/- 
per cylinder is in addition to the subsidy provided under the DBTL scheme. DBTL 
and PMUY schemes are distinct and operate independently.” 
1.24 Upon observing that in 2025–26, under the one-time grant, the actual 
expenditure was only Rs. 7,500 crore against the Budget Estimate (BE) of Rs. 12,500 
crore, yet the BE for 2026–27 has been raised to Rs. 17,500 crore, the Committee 
sought the factors justifying this increase, the changes involved, and the Ministry’s plan 
to ensure full utilization of the higher allocation and the Ministry responded with the 
following written reply: 
“The under-recoveries on domestic LPG (i.e. negative buffer balance) of the 
OMCs stood at Rs. 41,267 crore as on 31st March 2025. In view of the 
accumulated under-recoveries and the projected losses up to 31st March 2026, 
the Government approved compensation of Rs. 30,000 crore in August 2025, to 
be released in 12 equal tranches commencing from November 2025. 
Accordingly, during FY 2025–26, five tranches aggregating to Rs.12,500 crore 
are being released, while the balance amount of Rs.17,500 crore will be released 
in FY 2026–27 in the remaining seven tranches. 
Since the Cabinet, while approving the compensation package of Rs.30,000 
crore, stipulated a 12-tranche disbursement arrangement, the Budget provisions 
for FY 2025–26 and FY 2026–27 have been scheduled accordingly.”

1.28 The North East Gas Grid (NEGG) Natural Gas Pipeline Project is being

ONGC, GAIL, NRL & OIL, at an estimated cost of Rs. 9,265 crores in line with the 
Hydrocarbon Vision 2030 for the Northeast. The 1656 km grid, having a capacity of 4.75 
MMSCMD, will connect the eight northeastern states viz. Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, 
Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram and Sikkim and the regional gas 
sources to the National Gas Grid. The NEGG project on its implementation will ensure 
reliable and uninterrupted supply of natural gas supplies to consumers viz Industrial, 
Commercial, PNG (Domestic), CNG (Transport), etc. across the Northeast region. This 
key connectivity infrastructure network will not only ensure a reliable supply of natural 
gas to consumers but will also trigger cascading investments promoting industrial 
development while prioritizing environmental conservation. Govt. has approved Viability 
Gap Funding/Capital Grant of 60% of the Project Cost (Rs. 5559.00 Crores) for a period 
of five years.

1.29 On being asked about the repeat BE provision of Rs. 700 crores for this project in 
2026-27 as well against the underspending in 2025-26 and the hurdles faced in 
achieving the milestones under this project, the Ministry furnished the following written 
reply:  
“The BE of Rs 700 Cr for FY 2025-26 could not be met as the project is 
witnessing delay in ROU (Right of Use) acquisition due to the unavailability of 
land records, slow progress in getting permission from NHIDCL, and 
environmental vulnerabilities like flash floods and landslides, along with the 
declaration of force majeure conditions in Sikkim & Mizoram for a significant 
period of time. Due to the unavailability of ROU, the laying of the pipeline was 
greatly hampered during the peak period, and subsequently, the progress was 
affected in the monsoon season. Therefore, IGGL could not incur estimated 
CAPEX so as to demand Rs. 700 crore VGF as per BE (2025-26). Considering 
the cumulative CAPEX which IGGL can incur in NEGG during the FY 2025-26, 
the RE was reduced to Rs. 300 crore.The issues/hindrances obstructing CAPEX 
of the project hassince either been resolvedorat an advanced stage of resolution. 
Hence, IGGL is expected to achieve the expected CAPEX in 2026-27 and 
therefore BE for 2026-27 was proposed at 700 Crore. IGGL has incurred

When the Committee desired to know about the bottlenecks which led to low utilization 
under this scheme and the details of CBG projects that have received disbursement, the 
Ministry in its written reply submitted as under:  
“As on February 2026, the Project Appraisal Board (PAB) has approved 37 CBG 
projects with total Financial Assistance (FA) of ₹248 crore.

Aggregation Machinery (BAM) within six months of approval (extendable with

PART-II 
OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
1. Need for Prudent Budgeting 
 
The Committee note that during the FY 2023-24, against a total Budget 
Estimate (BE) of Rs.41,007.72 crore, the Revised Estimate (RE) was reduced to 
Rs.14,757.01 crore and the Actual Expenditure (AE) stood at Rs.14,330.21 crore, 
which is only about 34.9 per cent of BE but 97.1 per cent of RE. The Committee 
observe that in 2024-25, the situation somewhat improved with total BE of 
Rs.15,930.26 crore, RE of Rs.20,305.61 crore and AE of Rs.19,887.49 crore, 
resulting in AE standing at about 124.84 per cent of BE and 97.94 per cent of RE.  
 
Further, in 2025-26, with an enhanced BE of Rs.26,702.93 crore and a higher 
RE of Rs.32,934.47 crore, AE was Rs.17,074.19 crore, which corresponds to about 
63.94 per cent of BE and 51.84 per cent of RE.  The under-utilisation is also seen 
in the capital segment where AE of Rs.281.89 crore is 2.28 per cent of the capital 
BE of Rs.12,323.13 crore and 10.83 per cent of capital RE of Rs.2,601.26 crore. 
 
For FY 2026-27, the Ministry has proposed a total BE of Rs.37,653.22 crore, 
with Revenue BE at Rs.37,414.77 crore and a reduced Capital BE of Rs.238.45 
crore, indicating a significant increase in revenue allocation and a marked 
reduction in capital provision compared to previous years. The Committee are of 
the view that the ministry may adopt sound budgeting and forecasting models in 
order to minimize the wide variations in fund allocations and help in reducing 
last-minute surrenders and curtailment or topping-up of provisions at the RE 
stage. 
 
 
2. Enhanced Budgetary Support for Capital Expenditure 
 
The Committee note that the Ministry’s pattern of capital expenditure has 
been marked by volatility and significant under-utilisation of budgeted 

34 
 
provisions. In 2023–24, against a Budget Estimate of Rs.35,508.98 crore under the 
Capital Section, the Actual Expenditure was only Rs.40 crore (0.11 percent of BE), 
primarily because major heads such as ‘Capital support to OMC’ (BE Rs.30,000 
crore) and ‘Payment to ISPRL for Crude Oil Reserve’ (BE Rs.5,000 crore) recorded 
zero Actual Expenditure.  A similar pattern recurs in 2025–26 where the Capital 
BE of Rs.12,323.13 crore translated into an Actual Expenditure of only Rs.281.89 
crore (2.28 percent of BE), with key strategic heads like ISPRL crude oil reserves 
(BE Rs.5,597 crore) and transfers to the Oil Industry Development Fund (BE 
Rs.5,697 crore) again remaining largely unspent. There is reduction in the Capital 
BE to Rs.238.45 crore in 2026–27 against a Revenue BE of Rs.37,414.77 crore. 
Given the fact that Capital expenditure should be on the higher side as it 
creates long-lived public assets and delivers strong returns in terms of economic 
expansion and employment generation, the Committee recommend that the 
Ministry may endeavour to provide government budgetary support for capital 
expenditure in order to fructify the Union Government’s strategy of using 
infrastructure-led investment as the main driver of medium and long term growth.    
 
 
3. Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG 
 
The Committee note that expenditure under the Direct Benefit Transfer for 
LPG (DBTL) Scheme depends on the actual claims submitted by Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) towards net under-recoveries which in turn reflect 
international prices and net ocean freight. In 2024-25, extreme volatility in net 
ocean freight led to some negative bills from OMCs, resulting in a much lower net 
claim than in the previous year, so that against a BE of Rs. 1,500 crore, reduced 
to Rs. 500 crore at RE, actual expenditure was only Rs. 375.27 crore.  For 2025-26, 
an outlay of Rs. 1,500 crore at BE and Rs. 1,000 crore at RE has been provided 
but actual expenditure up to 31.12.2025 is nil because the Scheme is under 
appraisal by the Department of Expenditure (DoE) as it transitions to the next 
Finance Commission cycle. The Ministry has submitted a comprehensive 
proposal on 01.10.2025 for fresh appraisal and continuation of the DBTL Scheme, 
covering both existing commitments and future requirements, and has 
temporarily withheld settlement of part of the OMCs’ bills pending finalisation of 

35 
 
this appraisal, even though DBT transfers to beneficiaries have already taken 
place. Taking into account the accumulated but unsettled past claims of OMCs as 
well as expected future claims, an allocation of Rs. 1,500 crore has been provided 
in BE 2026-27 by the Ministry. 
 
The Committee, therefore, urge the Ministry to coordinate with DoE to 
secure early approval so that the pending claims can be cleared in a timely 
manner and the expenditure position for 2025-26 accurately reflects the 
committed liabilities and the 2026-27 BE allocation is justified with expeditious 
settlements thereby safeguarding OMC liquidity and ensuring uninterrupted 
delivery of subsidised LPG to consumers.  The Ministry has stated that 
corresponding DBT transfers have already been executed and credited to 
beneficiaries’ bank accounts.  The Committee may be furnished the details in this 
regard.  
 
The Committee also opine that in order to cushion LPG subsidies from 
extreme volatility in net ocean freight, the Ministry may explore the feasibility of 
developing a freight management framework that narrows year-to-year swings in 
net ocean freight, thereby smoothing DBTL subsidy claims, enabling more 
realistic BE and RE formulation and avoiding large negative adjustments or 
abrupt underspending that hinder fiscal planning. The Committee further suggest 
that the Ministry, in consultation with Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell 
(PPAC), OMCs and the Department of Expenditure, devise this framework through 
suitable contractual guidelines and monitoring arrangements. 
 
4.  LPG Connection to Poor Households (Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana) 
 
The Committee note that Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), launched 
in May 2016 to provide deposit-free LPG connections to poor women, has largely 
achieved saturation of LPG access, with 10.43 crore connections issued by 
01.01.2026 and another 25 lakh sanctioned for 2025-26, of which 10.35 lakh are 
already released. Budget utilisation has strengthened, with 100% utilisation of 
Revised Estimates in 2023-24 and 2024-25 and expected full utilisation in 2025-26 
through settlement of pending claims of Rs. 4,958 crore.  The Committee also 

36 
 
note that to improve budgeting and accounting, three separate heads have been 
created viz., (i) new PMUY connections, (ii) targeted subsidies to PMUY 
beneficiaries and (iii) PME/IEC ( Publicity, Monitoring & Evaluation/Information, 
Education and Communication) Campaign expenses.  The Committee find this a 
welcome step towards greater transparency.  While appreciating the 
achievements of the Ministry on PMUY, the Committee wish to underline that the 
main challenge now is sustaining LPG usage, especially in rural areas where over 
80% of PMUY connections are located. 
 
According to the Ministry, average per-connection consumption has 
increased from about 3.6–3.7 refills in 2021-22/2022-23 to roughly 4.8 refills 
(pro-rated) in 2025-26, with most States showing a similar upward trend, 
suggesting that the Rs 200, increased to Rs 300 later on, per-cylinder subsidy (up 
to nine refills) and programme outreach are having a positive impact.  However, 
the Committee are of the view that average usage of only 4–5 refills a year 
indicates that many households still do not rely on LPG as their primary cooking 
fuel throughout the year and inter-State differences—with some States at 5 or 
more refills and others at 3 to 4—show persistent pockets of low usage despite 
near-universal connections.  
 
The Ministry has stated that consumption of domestic LPG by households 
depends on several factors like food habits, household size, cooking habits, 
preferences, price, availability of alternate fules etc.  However, the Committee are 
aware that there is widespread evidence from independent evaluations that high 
effective refill cost, cash-flow constraints at the time of purchase, continued 
availability of solid fuels and service-delivery issues including lack of doorstep 
delivery and transaction costs may be acting as major impediments to sustained 
LPG use among low-income households. The Committee are of the view that 
unless these issues of affordability and refill behaviour are addressed 
systematically, PMUY may not become an effective instrument for durable 
transition to clean cooking fuels. The Committee, therefore recommend that:  
  

37 
 
 
(i) Considering the lower number of refills, the committee recommend that the 
Ministry may explore the feasibility of introduction of a targeted expansion of the 
LPG subsidy components, wherein regions which have lowest refill rates could 
be given a higher-than-average subsidy amount; 
(ii) sustained and affordable LPG availability among existing beneficiaries, 
particularly in rural and low-income areas may be ensured. The Ministry may use 
granular refill-behaviour data for the 10.43 crore PMUY consumers to identify the 
households that, despite holding a connection, are unable to use LPG regularly 
due to refill costs, liquidity constraints or local supply-chain issues.  The Ministry 
may, therefore, explore to design targeted interventions to ensure durable and 
meaningful access to clean cooking; 
(iii)  The Ministry may strengthen their monitoring framework for PMUY; and  
(iv)  The service-delivery aspects of PMUY may be substantially strengthened 
with particular emphasis on rural areas.  
 
5.  One-time Grant to OMCs 
 
The Committee observe that under the head ‘One-time Grant to PSU OMCs 
for under-recoveries in Domestic LPG’, against a Revised Estimate of Rs. 12,500 
crore in 2025-26, the actual expenditure is only Rs. 7,500 crore, whereas the BE 
for 2026-27 is enhanced to Rs. 17,500 crore. The Committee are informed that this 
flows from the Cabinet approval of an overall compensation package of Rs. 
30,000 crore, approved in August 2025 to be disbursed in 12 equal monthly 
tranches commencing from November 2025, of which five tranches fall in FY 
2025-26 and seven in FY 2026-27. The Committee note that as on 31.12.2025 the 
Ministry has spent Rs.7,500 crore. Since each tranche consist of Rs.2,500 crore, 
the Ministry may apprise whether they would be able to completely utilize the 
remaining Rs.5,000 crore by 31 March, 2026. The Committee are of the view that a 
realistic internal assessment at RE stage about whether all five scheduled 
tranches would be fully disbursed or booked in accounts by 31 March 2026 would 
have helped the Ministry in projecting its RE in line with realistic disbursement 
capacity. The Ministry may apprise the final details of the expenditure on this 
account during 2025-26, while furnishing action taken replies to the Committee. 

38 
 
 
Further, the Committee, suggest that timely disbursement of the 
sanctioned grant of Rs.17,500 for the year 2026-27 to OMCs may be made in order 
to enhance their financial strength and viability in the wake of constant volatility 
in oil prices. 
 6. Other Subsidy Payable Including North East Region (Domestic Natural Gas) 
 
The Committee note that under the head ‘subsidy payable including NE 
region’, the 2025-26 Budget Estimate was Rs. 1,200 crore, the Revised Estimate 
Rs. 1,103 crore and expenditure by February 2026 about Rs. 785.3 crore, 
reflecting subsidy on gas sales up to October 2025, with additional audited claims 
for November 2025 to February 2026 expected to be paid once the Department of 
Economic Affairs relaxes Quarterly and Monthly Expenditure Plans. The 
expenditure pattern of the scheme shows 100 % utilisation of BE/RE in 2023-24, 
91.97% of BE/RE in 2024-25 and 71.19 percent of RE in 2025-26.  The Ministry has 
assured that the entire allocation under RE 2025-26 will be fully utilised subject to 
the approval of the proposal sent to Budget Division, Department of Economic 
Affairs (DEA) for relaxation/revision of Quarterly Expenditure Plan (QEP)/Monthly 
Expenditure Plan (MEP).  
 
The Committee understand that North East (NE)-specific gas subsidies are 
used as a regional-equity instrument to provide affordable Administered Pricing 
Mechanism (APM) gas to industries and consumers in a geographically 
constrained region, thereby promoting industrial growth, jobs and cleaner fuel 
use. The Committee, urge the Ministry to follow up the matter so that settlement 
of all pending claims related to subsidy payable including NER may be made 
effective with a view to utilise the allocated funds.  The Committee also 
emphasize that the Ministry may periodically review and refine the coverage of 
the NE APM Gas Subsidy Scheme so that support is increasingly focused on 
priority, job-creating sectors and genuinely disadvantaged consumers in the 
North-Eastern Region, with clear caps in place.  
  

39 
 
 
7.  Indradhanush Gas Grid Limited 
 
The Committee note that the North East Gas Grid (NEGG) Natural Gas 
Pipeline Project of Indradhanush Gas Grid Limited (IGGL), envisaged to connect 
eight North Eastern states with a 1,656 km pipeline at an estimated cost of Rs 
9,265 crore with 60% Viability Gap Funding (VGF) which comes to Rs. 5,559 crore, 
has experienced substantial delays in execution. While the approved project cost 
and VGF quantum have not been revised, the timeline for release of VGF has 
been extended from 31.03.2025 to 31.03.2027, resulting in time overrun without 
cost overrun. 
 
The Ministry has attributed the underspending against the BE 2025-26 
provision of Rs 700 crore and RE of Rs 300 crore to the impact of Right of Use 
(RoU) acquisition difficulties, delays in permissions from National Highways and 
Infrastructure Development Corporation (NHIDCL) and other authorities and 
environmental vulnerabilities such as flash floods, landslides and force majeure 
conditions in Sikkim and Mizoram.  The Committee note that as of 31.12.2025, 
IGGL has incurred cumulative CAPEX of Rs 6,678 crore, with cumulative VGF 
sanctioned at Rs 4,414 crore and utilisation of Rs 4,383 crore indicating that the 
remaining works and VGF tranches are time-critical for realising project benefits. 
The Committee note that the project is falling behind its completion schedule. 
The Committee, therefore, emphasize to give due priority to this crucial 
infrastructure project and put in place a strengthened coordination mechanism 
with state governments and key agencies to fast-track RoU and statutory 
clearances, adopt targeted seasonal and terrain-sensitive construction planning 
wherever necessary and align budgetary provisions with realistic CAPEX 
trajectories.  Further, remaining VGF releases may be more closely linked to 
physical progress milestones while IGGL should implement dedicated RoU task 
forces, enhanced risk management for disaster-prone stretches and stakeholder 
engagement programmes to minimise local disruptions and ensure completion of 
NEGG by 31.03.2027 and early commissioning of completed sections, in order to 
realise Hydrocarbon Vision 2030 for North-East. 
 

40 
 
8. Indian Institute of Petroleum Energy (IIPE) 
 
The Committee note that the Indian Institute of Petroleum and Energy (IIPE) 
which was operating from a temporary campus in Andhra University, 
Vishakhapatnam since its inception in 2016, has shifted to a permanent campus 
in Anakapalli District on 05.01.2026.  The Committee also note that owing to a 
prolonged legal dispute, the land allotted free of cost by the Government of 
Andhra Pradesh for the Institute could be formally handed over to IIPE only in 
March 2023. As of 31.12.2025, Phase-I construction of IIPE has achieved about 
79% progress with essential academic and hostel buildings being completed.  
 
As regards the budget allocations for the project, the Committee note that 
although substantial Budget and Revised Estimates had been provided for the 
project, the actual release of funds in 2024–25 and 2025–26 remained 
constrained. In 2023–24 and 2024–25, the Budget Estimates (BE) were maintained 
at Rs. 168 crore for each year. The Revised Estimates (RE) were subsequently 
reduced to Rs. 90.00 crore and Rs. 88.08 crore respectively. While the entire RE 
allocation for 2023–24 was fully utilised, no expenditure was incurred during 
2024–25. The Ministry informed in this regard that as the construction of the 
Institute was delayed due to land litigation issues, timelines for release of capital 
outlay as approved by the Cabinet lapsed and hence, no fund could be released 
during FY 2024-25 due to pending extension of project’s timelines.  Further, BE 
2025-26 was 0.00 due to the same reason, and Rs.50.00 Crore have been allocated 
to IIPE in January, 2026 only, through 1st Supplementary Demand for Grants. 
 
The Committee hope that the Ministry will take adequate steps to fully 
utilize the allocated Rs.50 Crore of RE 2025-26 & Rs.302 Crore of BE 2026-27.  
 
9.  Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana 
 
The Committee note that the Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN (Jaiv Indhan–
Vatavaran Anukool Fasl Awashesh Nivaran) Yojana, launched in 2019, aims to 
provide financial support for advanced biofuel and 2G ethanol projects using 
lignocellulosic biomass and other renewable feedstock. Under the scheme, 14 
commercial and 8 demonstration proposals were received, of which 8 commercial 

41 
 
and 4 demonstration projects have been approved, though 3 commercial projects 
were later withdrawn by the developers. To attract wider participation, the 
scheme was amended in August 2024 to expand its scope from 2G ethanol to 
broader advanced biofuels, allow bolt-on plants and brownfield projects and the 
timeline was extended up to FY 2028-29. Following this amendment, 14 additional 
proposals have been received under Request for Selection (RFS-V) which are 
currently under review. 
 
The Committee also note that the budgetary allocations under the scheme 
have remained under-utilised. In 2023-24, against a BE of Rs.227.26 crore and RE 
of Rs.151.99 crore, the actual expenditure was Rs.75.75 crore (33.33% of BE).  In 
2024-25, against a BE of Rs.117.41 crore and RE of Rs.30 crore, Rs.7.575 crore 
(6.45% of BE) were spent.  In 2025-26, against a BE of 117.41, RE was reduced to 
Rs.37.88 crore which is expected to be released by the end of FY 2025-26.  For FY 
2026-27, Rs.196.94 crore has been allocated for the scheme. 
 
The Committee note that despite the efforts by the Ministry, out of 5 
approved commercial plants, only one commercial plant at Haryana has been 
commissioned as of now. Out of 4 Demonstration Projects, only one project at 
Haryana is mechanically completed.  Remaining projects are under various 
stages of completion. Considering the envisaged benefits of this ambitious 
Scheme, the Committee find its progress very slow.   
 
The Committee note that the scheme’s total outlay up to 2028-29 is 
Rs.1,969.5 crore. The Ministry has indicated that the number of commercial 
projects are expected to increase from 5 to 13 and demonstration projects from 4 
to 11, with the cumulative design capacity of advanced biofuels projected to 
increase from 17.66 crore litres in 2024-25 to 38.66 crore litres. The Committee are 
of the view that while projecting its budgetary requirements, the Ministry may 
look at better alignment between the financial allocation and the pace of project 
implementation. The Ministry may also ensure that administrative and procedural 
delays in release of financial assistance are minimised so that allocated funds are 
fully utilized.  
 

42 
 
The Committee note that the Ministry has attributed the under-utilisation of 
funds mainly to technological and operational challenges associated with 
advanced biofuel and 2G ethanol technologies which are still in early stages 
globally and the developers worldwide are facing challenges in biomass 
conversion. In view of the same, the Ministry may endeavour to promote greater 
collaboration with research institutions, technology providers and industry 
stakeholders to support technology validation, operational troubleshooting and  
 
knowledge sharing among project developers with a view to strengthen 
technology support and capacity building.  
 
The Committee note that 14 proposals received under RFS-V are currently 
under review and further proposals are expected under upcoming selection 
rounds. The Ministry should ensure expeditious evaluation and approval of viable 
proposals so that the expanded scope of the scheme translates into tangible 
capacity addition and improved utilisation of allocated funds. Further, in order to 
strengthen implementation of the Scheme, the Ministry may consider a time-
bound implementation framework with clearly defined milestones for each 
approved project and closely monitor progress to ensure timely commissioning 
of the remaining projects.  
 
 
10.  Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserve Limited - Strategic Crude Oil Reserve (O&M)  
 
The Committee note that the Government provides budgetary support to 
Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserve Limited (ISPRL) under the scheme “Payment 
to ISPRL for Strategic Crude Oil Reserve (O&M)” for meeting the Operations and 
Maintenance (O&M) expenses of Strategic Petroleum Reserve facilities 
(established under phase-I) located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur, 
having a total storage capacity of 5.33 MMT of crude oil. The Committee also note 
a gap between the Budget Estimates (BE), Revised Estimates and the Actual 
Expenditure (AE) under the scheme in the last three financial years with the 
actual expenditure standing at 75%, 45% and 47% of BE allocated in FYs.2023-24, 
2024-25 and 2025-26.  
 

43 
 
The Committee further note that the Ministry has attributed the reduction in 
expenditure to factors such as non-deployment of planned security personnel, 
lower electricity and manpower costs, delays in deputation of staff, lower crude 
oil operational activities and delays in finalising the warehousing agreement with 
Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited. 
 
While the Committee acknowledge that certain reductions may have arisen 
due to operational efficiencies and lower-than-estimated expenditure, they are of  
 
the opinion that recurring downward revisions from BE to RE indicate 
shortcomings in realistic assessment of operational requirements and planning. 
The Committee are of the opinion that given the strategic importance of crude oil 
reserves in strengthening the country’s energy security, such variations in 
budgeting merit closer examination. 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry may undertake a 
more realistic assessment of O&M requirements, particularly with regard to 
manpower deployment, security arrangements and operational agreements, so as 
to minimise wide variations between BE and RE. The Committee also urge the 
Ministry to expedite pending operational arrangements and contractual 
agreements so that the infrastructure created under the Strategic Petroleum 
Reserve programme is utilised efficiently and the budgetary allocations are 
optimally utilised.  
 
11. Payment to ISPRL for purchase of land 
 
The Committee note that a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was 
signed between Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL) and 
Mangalore Special Economic Zone Limited (MSEZL) on 17 March 2023 for 
acquisition of 154.90 acres of land by ISPRL from MSEZL for establishing 
additional cavern storage at its facility in Mangalore. As per the terms of the MoU, 
ISPRL was required to decide whether the proposed facilities would be developed 
under the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) or within the Special Economic Zone (SEZ) 
framework. Based on this decision, MSEZL was required to either de-notify 88.16 

44 
 
acres of land or notify 66.74 acres, together constituting the total area of 154.90 
acres. ISPRL decided to proceed with the option of notification of 66.74 acres of 
land and the decision was communicated to MSEZL on 18 June 2025.  An amount 
of Rs.215.59 crore has already been paid by ISPRL against a total cost of 
Rs.226.94 crore. However, the Committee note that the signing of deed with 
MSEZL is still pending due to the awaiting confirmation regarding notification of 
66.74 acres of land by MSEZL.  An amount of Rs.10 crore is allocated in 2026-27 
BE for purchase of land by ISPRL. 
 
The Committee are of the view that Strategic Petroleum Reserves play a 
crucial role in strengthening the energy security of the country. The Committee, 
therefore, emphasize that the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas pursue the 
matter with MSEZL and other authorities concerned on priority to expedite the 
notification of the remaining land and facilitate the early execution of the lease 
deed. Ministry may also ensure close coordination with all the stakeholders and 
establish a clear timeline for completion of the remaining formalities so that the 
development of additional cavern storage at Mangalore can commence at the 
earliest. 
 
  
12. Payment to ISPRL for Construction of Caverns Phase-II 
 
 
The Committee note that with a view to strengthening the country’s energy 
security, the Government approved the construction of two additional Strategic 
Petroleum Reserves (SPR) under Phase-II on 8 July 2021 with a total storage 
capacity of 6.5 MMT, comprising of 4 MMT at Chandikhol in Odisha and 2.5 MMT 
at Padur in Karnataka. Land acquisition of Chandikhol is at an advanced stage 
and financial closure is in progress to meet the conditions precedent as per the 
Concessionaire Agreement in Padur-II project.  
 
As regards budget allocation for the Scheme, the Committee observe that 
the allocation has been scaled down at the RE stage over the past three years.  
For the financial year 2023-24, an amount of Rs.508 crore was projected at the BE 
stage which was reduced to Rs.40 crore at RE but no expenditure could be 
incurred. In FY 2024–25, the BE was Rs.408.00 crore which was reduced to 

45 
 
Rs.30.00 crore at the RE stage and an expenditure of Rs.17.25 was incurred. In FY 
2025–26, the BE was Rs.100.00 crore, which was revised downward to Rs.20.00 
crore at the RE stage with expenditure standing at Rs.14.54 crore . For 2026-27, 
Rs. 20 crore is allocated for the project. 
 
The Committee are of the view that scaling down Budget Estimates may be 
avoided and projects may get off the ground as fast as they should. The 
Committee note that delays in finalising the bidding process and subsequent 
stages under the PPP framework led to the withdrawal of funds projected for 
milestone payments at the BE stage, particularly for the Phase-II project at Padur 
in Karnataka. The Committee are of the view that the Ministry may project realistic 
and need-based budgeting, taking into account the actual progress of land 
acquisition, readiness of project implementation and contractual milestones at 
the BE stage itself. 
 
 
The Committee, while taking note of the reasons furnished by the Ministry, 
are of the view that in projects of strategic national importance, the allocated 
funds may be fully utilized. The Committee, therefore, urge the Ministry to ensure 
better planning, timely execution and optimal utilisation of funds so that the 
objectives of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve programme are achieved within the 
stipulated timeframe. The Committee also recommend to the Ministry/OMCs to 
explore the possibility of constructing more such caverns across the country 
wherever geological conditions are favourable keeping in view the overall energy 
security of the country.  
 
Furthermore, in light of the global energy crisis arising from current 
geopolitical situations, the Committee strongly urge the Ministry to make every 
possible effort to achieve the global standard of maintaining 90 days of crude oil 
storage within the country for strengthening the nation’s energy security and 
safeguarding the economy against potential supply shocks and external 
uncertainties. 
  

46 
 
 
 
13. Financial Support for collection of Bio-Mass 
 
The Committee note that the Scheme for Providing Financial Assistance to 
Compressed Bio Gas (CBG) producers for procurement of Biomass Aggregation 
Machinery (BAM) was launched on 9 January 2024 and so far, 37 CBG projects 
have received in-principle approval with a total Financial Assistance (FA) of 
Rs.248 crore approved by the Project Appraisal Board (PAB). The Committee also 
note that despite a Budget Estimate (BE) of Rs.150 crore during FY 2024–25 and 
FY 2025–26, the actual expenditure has remained significantly low at Rs.1.72 
crore and Nil expenditure (as on 31.12.2025) respectively, even though the 
scheme has an overall outlay of Rs.564.75 crore for the period 2023–24 to 2026–
27. 
 
The Committee are informed that the low utilization of funds is primarily 
due to non-submission of claims by beneficiaries, as disbursement is contingent 
upon the procurement of Biomass Aggregation Machinery (BAM) and submission 
of the required documents. The Committee also note that only one claim has 
been received so far, resulting in Rs.1.72 crore being released in FY 2024–25, 
while Rs.4.37 crore for the same project is under process in FY 2025–26. The 
Committee further take note of the Ministry’s submission that several 
beneficiaries are still in the process of procuring machinery or have sought 
extensions. 
 
While acknowledging the revision of the scheme in July 2025 which 
broadened eligibility criteria, reduced the minimum physical progress 
requirement from 50% to 25% for eligibility and introduced mobilization advance, 
the Committee are of the view that the pace of implementation of the Scheme 
remains slow. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry may take 
proactive measures to expedite procurement of Biomass Aggregation Machinery 
by approved CBG projects, facilitate timely submission of claims and ensure 
faster disbursement of Financial Assistance under the scheme. The Ministry may 
also closely monitor the progress of approved projects, address procedural 

47 
 
bottlenecks and undertake greater outreach and handholding of beneficiaries so 
that the intended objective of supporting 100 agri-residue based CBG projects 
and promoting effective utilization of agricultural residues is achieved within the 
stipulated timeframe.  
 
 
14. Scheme for Development of Pipeline Infrastructure for injection of Compressed 
Bio Gas (CBG) in City Gas Distribution Network. 
 
The Committee note that the Scheme for Development of Pipeline 
Infrastructure (DPI) for injection of Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) into the City Gas 
Distribution (CGD) network was approved on 15th March, 2024 with the objective 
of ensuring full off-take of CBG through cost-effective pipeline transportation 
from production facilities to consumption centres. The Committee further note 
that the scheme guidelines were issued on 26th June, 2024 and the application 
portal was activated from 1st September, 2024. As informed by the Ministry, the 
Project Appraisal Board has so far approved 24 projects amounting to Rs.56.31 
crore and these projects are expected to be connected to CGD networks by the 
year 2026-27, subject to completion of pipeline laying within the stipulated time 
frame. 
 
The Committee also note the gap between the Budget Estimate (Rs.250 
crore) and the actual expenditure (Rs.0.91 crore) under the scheme in FY 2025-26. 
The Committee note the Ministry’s explanation that financial assistance under the 
scheme is released only after commissioning of the pipeline and that most of the 
sanctioned projects are still under construction, with only five projects having 
received partial disbursement upon achieving the 50 per cent milestone.  
 
The Committee take note of the Ministry’s decision to revise the scheme 
guidelines in August, 2025 to allow connectivity not only with CGD networks but 
also with trunk pipelines through a cluster-based approach and to provide for 
mobilisation advance as well as milestone-based financial assistance. The 
Committee consider these modifications as positive steps to address the earlier 
limitations of the scheme, particularly in areas where CGD demand was 
insufficient to absorb the entire CBG output. 

48 
 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry may closely 
monitor the progress of the approved projects and ensure that pipeline 
infrastructure is completed within the stipulated timelines so that the targeted 
connectivity to CGD or trunk pipelines by 2026-27 is achieved. The Committee 
further urge the Ministry to strengthen coordination with CBG producers, CGD 
entities and other stakeholders to expedite project execution and avoid delays in 
submission of claims for financial assistance. The Committee also recommend 
that periodic awareness programmes and stakeholder consultations may be 
continued to enhance participation under the scheme and ensure optimal 
utilisation of the allocated funds.  
  
15. Expansion of PNG Connections  
 
The Committee observe that in recent times, PNG (Piped Natural Gas) 
connections have emerged as an effective alternative to LPG cylinders, especially 
in larger cities of Delhi and Mumbai due to higher convenience and flexibility for 
domestic consumers and also because PNG connections are considered safer. 
The Committee note that the target for PNG connections by the year 2034 is over 
12 crores, however, the number of PNG connections currently is much lower. The 
Committee, therefore, are of the opinion that the Ministry may explore the 
possibility of according priority for expanding PNG connections in the form of 
CGD (City Gas Distribution) network.

16.  Mission Anveshan 
 
The Committee note that Mission Anveshan, launched as a continuation of 
the National Seismic Program, envisages acquisition, processing and 
interpretation of 20,275 Line Kilometres (LKM) of 2D seismic data across seven 
onshore sedimentary basins namely Rajasthan, Ganga-Punjab, Chhattisgarh, 
Cuddapah, Krishna-Godavari, Deccan Syneclise and Saurashtra with an approved 
outlay of Rs.792 crore and is scheduled for completion by FY 2026–27. The 
Committee have been informed that 10,663.44 LKM of seismic data has been 
acquired as on 31 December 2025 which constitutes more than half of the 
targeted survey work.  
 
The Committee also take note that the work is being carried out by Oil and 
Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Oil India Limited (OIL) and out of 10,663.44 
Line Kilo Meter (LKM) data, ONGC acquired 4,179.62 LKM and OIL acquired 
6843.82 LKM.  Further, OIL has awarded the Processing and Interpretation (P&I) 
contract while ONGC is currently in the process of issuing tender for its P&I work. 
The Committee also note that the Budget Estimate for FY 2025–26 was revised 
from Rs.592 crore to Rs.200 crore due to delayed award of contracts with 
Rs.107.03 crore utilisation as on 31.12.2025. Further, bills amounting to Rs.39.44 
crore, though concurred by the Internal Finance Division, are yet to be 
reimbursed, pending exemption from the Department of Economic Affairs for 
release of funds.  
 
 While appreciating the Ministry for the commendable progress made under 
the Scheme, the Committee recommend that the Ministry may ensure timely 
completion of the remaining seismic survey work and expedite pending payments 
awaiting clearance from the Department of Economic Affairs.  Further, ONGC may 
accelerate its tendering process so that targets under Mission Anveshan are 
achieved within the stipulated timeline and a stronger, more reliable domestic 
energy base for future growth is built for the Country.

1 Oil & Natural Gas 
Corporation 
Limited (ONGC) 
ONGC, a Maharatna Schedule “A” CPSE under the administrative 
control of MoPNG, is a global energy major with a fully integrated 
presence across the entire energy value chain. As India’s largest 
Exploration & Production (E&P) company, ONGC has played a 
pivotal role in the nation’s energy security-having discovered 
seven of the country’s eight producing basins, accounting for 
nearly 83% of India’s hydrocarbon reserves and contributing 
approximately 63% of domestic hydrocarbon production. 
  
Through its subsidiaries and JVs, ONGC has built a diversified 
and robust footprint across upstream, midstream, downstream, 
power and emerging energy segments. Its wholly owned 
subsidiary, ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL), a Navratna Schedule 
“A” CPSE, serves as its international arm, driving global E&P 
activities. ONGC also maintains a strong downstream presence 
through its refinery and petrochemical subsidiaries, including 
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), Mangalore 
Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL), and ONGC Petro 
Additions Limited (OPAL). In line with its commitment to 
sustainability and energy transition, ONGC has further expanded 
into the green energy domain through its wholly owned subsidiary, 
ONGC Green Limited (OGL). 
 
ONGC has been able to maintain stable Crude oil & Natural gas 
production during FY’25. The standalone Crude production for 
FY’25 stood at 19.558 MMT, reflecting a 0.9% increase over the 
previous year. The standalone Natural gas production for FY’25 
stood at 19.654 BCM. 
2 ONGC Videsh 
Ltd (OVL), 
ONGC Videsh Ltd (OVL), a wholly owned subsidiary of ONGC, 
has been granted Navratna CPSE status and became the 14th 
Navratna in India. As ONGC’s overseas arm under the Ministry of 
Petroleum & Natural Gas, OVL focuses on exploration, 
development, and production of oil and gas outside India. It holds 
participating interests in 32 assets across 15 countries and is 
India’s second-largest petroleum company after parent ONGC 
with respect to both reserves and production. 
  
During FY2024-25, ONGC Videsh produced 10.278 Million 
Metric Tons of Oil Equivalent (MMtoe) of oil and gas, which is 
equivalent to about 15.9% of India’s domestic oil and gas 
production. 
3 Oil India Limited 
(OIL) 
OIL is a leading upstream oil and gas company with over six 
decades of hydrocarbon exploration experience, accounting for 
approximately 10% of the country’s total crude oil and natural gas 

53 
 
production. The company has a strong presence across the entire 
hydrocarbon value chain: Exploration, Production, Liquefied 
Petroleum Gas (LPG) and transporting crude oil and refined 
products via cross-country pipelines. Additionally, OIL is 
expanding into new energy sectors, including renewable energy, 
bio-fuels and Green Hydrogen, while maintaining its leadership in 
traditional hydrocarbon sectors. 
 
The authorized capital of OIL is ₹ 2,000 Crore and the paid up 
capital is ₹ 1626.61 Crore. As on 31.03.2025, Government of 
India’s shareholding is 56.66% of the paid-up equity share capital 
of OIL. 
4 GAIL (India) 
Limited (GAIL) 
GAIL is a Maharatna CPSE under the Ministry of Petroleum & 
Natural Gas.  GAIL business consists of transmission and 
marketing of Natural Gas and GAIL is also involved in production 
of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) and other liquid hydrocarbons, 
LPG transmission, Polymer production and marketing, City Gas 
Distribution, LNG sourcing, shipping and re-gasification, 
renewable energy initiatives and upstream exploration and 
production activities. It had a turnover of Rs. 1,36,960 crore 
during 2024-25. 
  
GAIL has a large network of Natural Gas pipelines of ~ 16,420 
Km; LPG Pipeline of ~ 2040 Km; five Gas Processing plants for 
production of LPG and other liquid hydrocarbons with a combined 
production capacity of around 1.4 MMTPA and a gas based 
integrated petrochemical plant of capacity 810 KTPA of polymer. 
 
GAIL is a pioneer in city gas distribution (CGD) business in India. 
It has presence in 72 Geographical Areas across India after 
completion of 12th CGD Bidding round.  GAIL has 8 JVs and 
three subsidiaries in India for its CGD business. 
5 Indian Oil 
Corporation 
Limited (IOCL) 
Indian Oil is India's flagship Maharatna national oil company with 
business interests straddling the entire hydrocarbon value chain-
from refining, pipeline transportation & marketing, to exploration 
& production of crude oil & gas, petrochemicals, gas marketing, 
alternative energy sources and globalisation of downstream 
operations. It is pursuing diverse business interests with the setting 
up of joint ventures with reputed business partners from India and 
abroad to explore global opportunities. 
  
It strong network includes10 group refineries, a 20,000+ km 
pipeline network, and 64,000+ customer touch points, ensuring 
efficient and uninterrupted operations. 
  
IOCL, having a combined refining capacity of around 70.3 
MMTPA, had a turnover of Rs. 8,40,842 crore during 2024-25. 
6 Bharat Petroleum 
Corporation 
Limited (BPCL) 
Bharat Petroleum (Fortune Global 500 Company) is the second 
largest Indian Oil Marketing Company and one of the integrated 
energy companies in India, engaged in refining of crude oil and 

54 
 
marketing of petroleum products, with presence in the upstream 
and downstream sectors of the oil and gas industry.  
  
Bharat Petroleum’s Refineries at Mumbai, Kochi and Bina have a 
combined refining capacity of around 35.3 MMTPA. It had a 
turnover of Rs. 4,98,869 crore during 2024-25. 
 
Its marketing infrastructure includes a network of installations, 
depots, energy stations, aviation service stations, LPG and Lubes 
distributors. Its distribution network comprises over 23,642 
Energy Stations, over 6,269 LPG distributorships, over 500 Lubes 
distributorships, and 80 POL storage locations, 54 LPG Bottling 
Plants, 73 Aviation Service Stations, 5 Lube blending plants and 5 
cross-country pipelines as on 31.03.2025. 
7 Hindustan 
Petroleum 
Corporation 
Limited (HPCL)  
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) is a Maharatna 
CPSE engaged in refining and marketing of petroleum products 
and a subsidiary of ONGC, incorporated on 15 July 1974. Its 
present installed refining capacity is 35.8 MMTPA.  
  
The company operates refineries at Mumbai and Visakhapatnam, 
has stakes in HMEL and MRPL, and runs India’s second-largest 
petroleum product pipeline network of 5,440 km. HPCL has an 
extensive marketing and distribution network, including over 
24,500 retail outlets and 6,389 LPG distributorships serving 9.8 
crore LPG consumers, and is supported by its HP Green R&D 
Centre while remaining committed to sustainability and CSR 
initiatives. 
 
During FY 2024–25, HPCL recorded gross sales of ₹4,64,247 
crore and a standalone PAT of ₹7,365 crore, with ONGC holding 
of 54.9% equity as of March 2025. HPCL achieved its highest-
ever sales volume of 49.8 MMT, crude processing of 25.3 MMT 
with 109% refinery capacity utilization, and pipeline throughput of 
26.9 MMT, commanding about 20.3% market share in India. 
8 Mangalore 
Refinery & 
Petrochemicals 
Limited (MRPL)  
MRPL is a Schedule-A Miniratna company under the Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural gas and a subsidiary of ONGC.   MRPL has 
about 6% Refining capacity share in India. The present installed 
refining capacity of MRPL is 15 MMTPA while it had a turnover 
of Rs. 1,09,239 crore during 2024-25. 
 
The main functions of the company is Refining and Marketing. 
MRPL procures Crude oil domestically and Internationally and 
produces various Petroleum Fuels and Petrochemicals. The 
Petroleum products produced are viz. LPG, Naphtha, various 
grades of Petrol, Aviation turbine Fuel(ATF), MTO (Mineral 
Turpentine Oil), Diesel, Fuel Oil, Bitumen, Pet-coke, Sulphur and 
Petrochemicals viz. Polypropylene, Paraxylene, Benzene & 
Toulene. Around 65% of the products are sold within the country. 
The balance products after meeting the domestic demand are 
exported. 

55 
 
 
Apart from Refining MRPL is also focused on Research and 
Development with focus on-  
 
1)  Process Integration  
2) Production of value added streams from Refinery streams  
3)  AI & ML for process improvements. 
9 Chennai 
Petroleum 
Corporation 
Limited (CPCL)  
CPCL, formerly known as Madras Refineries Limited (MRL), is a 
Schedule-A Miniratna company under the Ministry of Petroleum 
and Natural gas (MoPNG) and a subsidiary of IOCL. CPCL 
refines Crude oil to produce Petroleum products and is one of the 
most complex refineries with Fuel, Lube, Wax and Petrochemical 
feedstock production facilities. 
  
The present installed refining capacity of CPCL is 10.5 MMTРА. 
It had a turnover of Rs. 71,050 crore during 2024-25. 
10 Numaligarh 
Refineries Limited 
(NRL)  
Numaligarh Refinery Limited (NRL) is a Navaratna Public Sector 
Enterprise under the administrative control of Ministry of 
Petroleum & Natural Gas. NRL is a subsidiary of Oil India 
Limited (OIL) with a 3.0 MMTPA petroleum refinery at 
Numaligarh in Golaghat district of Assam. Present shareholding 
pattern of NRL is Oil India Limited (OIL)– 69.63%, Govt. of 
Assam (GoA) – 26% and Engineers India Limited (EIL) – 4.37%. 
It had a turnover of Rs. 25,144 crore during 2024-25. 
 
NRL’s refinery has a high complexity factor owing to advanced 
secondary processing technologies that has enabled achievement 
of high distillate yield. Product slate of NRL comprises LPG, 
Naphtha, Motor Spirit, Aviation Turbine Fuel, High Speed Diesel, 
Superior Kerosene Oil, Paraffin Wax, Raw/ Calcined Petroleum 
Coke and Sulphur. NRL has the largest Wax producing unit in the 
country. 
 
Recently a (2G) Bio-Refinery Plant at Numaligarh Refinery 
Limited (NRL), which uses bamboo as feedstock, was inaugurated 
by the Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi, on 14th September 
2025. 
11 Engineers India 
Limited (EIL) 
Engineers India Limited (EIL), established in 1965, is a Navratna 
CPSE under the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas and has 
been a key contributor to India’s hydrocarbon infrastructure and 
nation-building. Over the past six decades, EIL has evolved into a 
global “Total Solutions” engineering consultancy and project 
execution organization, known for operational excellence, quality, 
innovation, and sustainable development.  
  
With experience of over 8,000 assignments, including around 600 
major projects valued at more than USD 200 billion, EIL has 
implemented projects across the entire hydrocarbon value chain 
and has also diversified into urban solutions, infrastructure, data 
centres, mining and metallurgy, alternative fuels, green hydrogen 

56 
 
and ammonia, coal gasification, water and waste treatment, 
defence, ports and terminals, renewables, etc. 
12 Balmer Lawrie & 
Co Limited (BLC) 
BLC is a Category-I Mini Ratna Central Public Sector Enterprises 
(CPSE) under MoP&NG. The company is a diversified 
conglomerate with a presence in both manufacturing and services 
sectors. It manufactures Greases and Lubricants, Industrial 
Packaging and Chemicals while in the services segment the 
Company is engaged in providing services in the field of Logistics 
(which includes Freight Forwarding, Container Freight Stations 
and Temperature Controlled Warehouses), Travel and Vacations 
and Refinery & Oil Field Services (mainly in cleaning sludge and 
tanks in the oil and gas sector). The entire business of the 
Company has been organised under nine Strategic Business Units 
(SBU). 
  
The Company achieved Net Turnover of ₹ 2577.63 crore during 
2024-25 and the Profit before Tax of ₹ 313.79 Crore in 2024-25. 
13 Brahmaputra 
Cracker and 
Polymer Limited 
(BCPL) – 
subsidiary of 
GAIL 
BCPL is the largest petrochemical complex in the North Eastern 
Region, commissioned on 2 January 2016. The plant produces and 
supplies various grades of high-quality polymers across India and 
also exports to Bangladesh and Bhutan. GAIL (India) Limited, the 
principal promoter and majority shareholder with a 70% equity 
stake, markets BCPL’s products. The remaining 30% equity is 
equally held by Oil India Limited, Numaligarh Refinery Limited, 
and the Government of Assam. The company is an outcome of the 
historic Assam Accord and was incorporated to advance socio-
economic development in Assam and the North-East region.  
Other Organisations 
14 Oil Industry 
Development 
Board (OIDB) 
OIDB was established on 13th January, 1975 under the Oil 
Industry (Development) Act, 1974 to provide financial and other 
assistance for the development of Oil Industry.  The functions of 
the Board, as defined in Section 6 of the Act, involve rendering 
financial assistance including loans and grants for the promotion 
of all such activities as are, in its opinion, conducive to the 
development of the Oil Industry. 
 
During the year 2024-25, OIDB had released a total grant of 
Rs.264.13 crore till 31.03.2025 to regular grantee institutions viz. 
Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH), Centre for High 
Technology (CHT), Oil Industry Safety Directorate (OISD) and 
Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) and Indian 
Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd. (ISPRL), wholly-owned 
subsidiary of OIDB, for pre-project activities of Phase-II SPRs. 
15 Oil Industry 
Safety Directorate 
(OISD) 
OISD, established in 1986, is a technical directorate under the 
MoP&NG. It has been entrusted with the responsibility of 
formulating standards and overseeing its implementation through 
safety audits to enhance safety levels and reduce risk inherent with 
this industry.  OISD also acts as the regulator for safety in 
offshore. OISD standards are implemented on self-regulatory basis 
by the Oil & Gas companies. 

57 
 
16 Centre for High 
Technology 
(CHT) 
CHT acts as the Technical Wing of MoP&NG for implementation 
of scientific and technological programmes of Govt. of India.  
Major functions of CHT include: 
 
 Performance Benchmarking of Refineries, Petrochemicals and 
Pipelines 
 Performance improvement in Refineries through Best 
Practices, Special Studies, Operational Improvement and 
Process Technology. 
 Energy Efficiency Improvement in Downstream Hydrocarbon 
Sector 
 Petroleum Product Quality Improvement 
 Integration with Alternative Energies and New Initiatives in 
Downstream Sector for Future Sustainability 
 Promotion innovations and R&D in Downstream Hydrocarbon 
Sector including Hydrogen Research.  Coordination of 
activities of Scientific Advisory Committee (SAC) on 
Hydrocarbons of MoP&NG 
 Development of import substitute fuels, chemicals and 
catalysts 
 Nodal agency for 
a. Implementation of PM JI-VAN Yojana  
b. Implementation of SIGHT-2B scheme 
c. Implementation of scheme for “Financial assistance to 
Compressed Biogas (CBG) producers for procurement of 
biomass aggregation machinery (BAM)” 
d. Implementation of scheme for “Development of Pipeline 
Infrastructure (DPI) for facilitation of CBG Offtake”. 
 Management of GOBARdhan portal of MoPNG for CBG 
 Sharing of Best Practices and Information & Knowledge 
dissemination. 
17 Petroleum 
Planning & 
Analysis Cell 
(PPAC) 
PPAC was established as an attached office of MoPNG w.e.f. 1st 
April 2002 after dismantling the Administered Pricing Mechanism 
(APM) in the petroleum sector and abolition of the erstwhile Oil 
Coordination Committee (OCC). PPAC functions with the vision 
of being an authentic source for data and policy analysis in the 
hydrocarbon sector, which are: 
 
 Maintenance of an information data bank on oil and gas sector. 
 Analysing trends in the international oil market & domestic 
prices 
 POL demand forecasting 
 Conducting studies in the Oil & Gas and Energy Sector 
 Petroleum import and export trends 
 To provide inputs to Government particularly on pricing of 
petroleum products and administration of subsidy schemes 
including PMUY. 
 Administration of the subsidy schemes. 
18 Directorate DGH was set up under the administrative control of the MoP&NG. 

58 
 
General of 
Hydrocarbons 
(DGH) 
The objective of DGH is to promote sound management of the 
Indian petroleum and natural gas resources having a balanced 
regard for the environment, safety, technological and economic 
aspects of the petroleum activity. DGH has been entrusted with 
multifaceted functions and responsibilities, which, inter-alia, 
include: 
 
a) Providing technical expertise and advice to the Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas on pertinent issues related to the 
exploration and optimal exploitation of hydrocarbons in India and 
abroad by national oil companies. 
b) Scrutinizing and assessing the exploration programs of 
companies holding Petroleum Exploration Licenses (PELs) under 
the oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 and the 
Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules, 1959, with a view to advising 
the Government on the adequacy of these programs.  
c) Re-evaluating the estimated and discovered hydrocarbon 
reserves in coordination with the operating companies.  
d) Advising the Government on the allocation of exploration 
acreages to companies and matters concerning the relinquishment 
of such acreages.  
e) Reviewing the development plans proposed by operating 
companies for commercial discoveries of hydrocarbon reserves, 
assessing the feasibility of these plans and the proposed 
exploitation rates, and making recommendations to the 
Government.  
f) Concurrently reviewing and monitoring the management of 
petroleum reservoirs by operating companies and advising on any 
corrective actions required to ensure optimal exploitation of 
reserves and conservation of petroleum resources.  
g) Regulating the storage, maintenance and preservation of data 
and samples related to petroleum exploration, drilling, and 
production, and preparing data packages for the allocation of 
exploration acreages to companies.  
h) Undertaking other incidental functions and any other 
responsibilities as assigned by the Government from time to time. 
19 Petroleum and 
Natural Gas 
Regulatory Board 
(PNGRB) 
PNGRB was constituted under the PNGRB Act, 2006. The Act 
provides for the  establishment of PNGRB to protect the interests 
of consumers and  entities engaged in specified activities relating 
to  petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas and to promote 
competitive markets and for matters connected therewith or 
incidental thereto. The Board under the Act has to regulate the 
refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, 
marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and natural 
gas excluding production of crude oil and natural  gas so as to 
ensure uninterrupted and adequate supply of petroleum,  petroleum 
products and natural gas in all parts of the country. 
20 Indian Strategic 
Petroleum 
Reserves Limited 
India is heavily dependent on import of crude oil to support the 
economic activities and growth and to meet the energy needs of its 
citizens, these SPRs would serve as buffer to deal with any 

59 
 
(ISPRL) situation of supply chain disruptions, especially due to external 
reasons. Such emergency reserves would enable the country to 
keep its refineries fed with crude oil even in the face of disruption 
of crude oil imports and ensure uninterrupted supplies of 
petroleum products across the country. In exceptional 
circumstances, the buffer stock of crude oil could be used to 
partially absorb an abnormal spike, emergencies such as global 
supply shortages or geopolitical crises in the global oil prices. 
 
Government of India (GoI) in the interest of meeting the strategic 
objective of country’s energy security, decided on 7th January 
2004 to construct Strategic Petroleum Reserves (SPRs) facilities. 
To implement the decision of Govt. of India, under phase-I, to 
construct SPR facilities, a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) Indian 
Strategic Petroleum Reserve Limited (ISPRL) was established on 
16th June 2004 as a subsidiary of Indian Oil Corporation Limited. 
Subsequently in January 2006, ISPRL became a wholly owned 
subsidiary of Oil Industry Development Board (OIDB).

CHAPTER I 
 
REPORT 
 
 This Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the Government 
on the recommendations and obse rvations contained in the 20 th R e p o r t  o f  t h e  
Standing Committee on Railways (2005-06) on ‘Demands fo r Grants (2006-07)’ of the 
Ministry of Railways.  The Report was presented in Lok Sabha on 23.5.2006 and laid in 
Rajya Sabha simultaneously.  
 
1.2 Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of all 
the 14 recommendations/observations contai ned in the Report.  These have been 
broadly categorized as follows:- 
 
(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government – Para 
Nos.  1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14. 
    
(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do not desire to pursue in view 
of the Government’s replies – Para No. 13.    
 
(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not 
been accepted by the Committee and which require reiteration - Para Nos. 6 & 12. 
 
(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies are still awaited  Para 
N o s .  –  n i l .      
 
1.3. The Committee will now deal with the Action Taken by Government on 
    some of their recommendations/observations. 
A. X Five Year Plan 
(Recommendation Para No.1) 
1.4 The Committee had observed in the above  paragraph that the X Five Year Plan 
f o r  t h e  R a i l w a y s  w a s  a p p r o v e d  b y  t h e  P l a n n i n g  C o m m i s s i o n  w i t h  a n  o u t l a y  o f  R s .  
60,600 crore comprising Rs. 27,600 crore fr om Gross Budgetary Support and Rs. 
33,000 crore from Internal Resources & Mark et Borrowings.  The objectives of the 
Plan were inter-alia to strengthen the high  density network, build up capacity through 
National Rail Vikas Yojana, upgrade technological assets  for improving efficiency, 
improve safety of operations by replacem ent of over aged assets, utilization of 
information technology for be tter customer interface and complete sanctioned rail 
projects.   However, they found that in the terminal year i.e. 2006-07 the financial 

 7 
 
targets of the Plan were likely to be Rs. 82,674 crore consisting of Rs. 36,935 crore as 
Budgetary Support and Rs. 45,739 crore as Internal Resources and market borrowings 
resulting in 36 per cent increase in outlay as compared to the original plan outlay.    
 
1.5 As against this phenomenal increa se in financial outlay the physical 
achievement proposed under the Plan was no t likely to be achieved except under the 
Plan Heads Track Renewals, Gauge Conversion and Rolling Stocks.  The targets fixed 
under Plan Heads – New Lines and Doublings  were not likely to be achieved as 
proposed in the Plan.  The targets for Ne w Lines likely to be achieved were 1225 kms 
as against proposed target of 1310 kms.  Under Doubling the likely achievement was 
1417 kms as against 1500 kms.  An indepth stud y of the financial and physical targets 
fixed under the X Plan indica ted that even after an incr ease of about 36 per cent in 
the financial targets, the Railways were not able to achieve the originally envisaged 
physical targets.  However, the targets under Rolling Stock were most likely to 
outnumber the originally proposed targets except in case of Electric Multiple Units 
(EMUs).  It showed that the Railways did no t adhere to their obj ectives enshrined in 
the Plan and rather gave more importance to  increase their carrying capacity instead 
of expansion of their networ k.  The Committee were of the considered view that 
Railways needed expansion of their network in an expeditious way to decongest the 
traffic on highly saturated routes.  They  had, therefore, recommended that the 
Railways must accord utmost priority fo r the expansion and augmentation of rail 
network by completing all ongoing projects a s  e a r l y  a s  p o s s i b l e .    T h e y  f u r t h e r  
reiterated their earlier r ecommendation made in the 6 th Report (14 th Lok Sabha) for 
declaration of Bogibeel mega bridge and Rangia-Murkong-Selek (Gauge Conversion) 
projects as National Project.   
 
1.6 In their Action Taken Reply, the Minist ry of Railways have stated as under:  
 
“The Committee has acknowledged the achievement under the Planheads of 
Track Renewals and Gauge Conversions.  Ho wever, there will be some shortfall in 
meeting the targets of New Lines and Doubli ng Plan heads.  The concern expressed 
by the Committee has been noted and effo rts are being made to complete the 
doublings on saturated routes in a time bound manner. A thrust has been given in 

 8 
 
implementation of doublings and other throughput enhancem ent works and large 
number of these works have been transferred to Rail Vikas Nigam Limited. 
  
 Certain changes have also been brou ght out in the General Conditions of 
Contract and the same is likely to have positive effect in selection of capable 
contractors and fast remedial action in case of failure of contractor in satisfactorily 
progressing the work. 
 
 It is a fact that outlays for projects ha ve increased considerably over the years, 
however, funds are being distributed as per the Statewise formula keeping in view the 
overall priority of the project.  This has re sulted into taking up of large number of 
projects requiring more funds fo r even the non-targeted proj ects.  Actually, in such a 
scenario with large number of projects having heavy throwforward, the increase in 
outlay do not get translated commensurate into the physical targets. 
 
 In order to expedite completion of pr ojects, number of initiatives have been 
taken to generate additional resources apart from normal budgetary support.  Ministry 
of Railways have requested Chief Ministers of the State Governments to share atleast 
50% of the cost of ongoing New Line and Gauge Conversion  projects in their States 
which have been taken up primarily on so cio-economic considerat ions.  Further, to 
bring down the unit cost of construction of the rail line, lower signaling and track 
standards have been prescribed  for the lines having low proj ected traffic.  It is hoped 
that these measures would help in expediting the completion of projects. 
 
 As regards declaration of Bogibeel Rail Cum Road Bridge and Rangia-Murkong-
Selek Gauge Conversion project as National Projects, it is mentioned that the proposal 
was considered by the Government and it has been directed th at the projects be 
implemented through SPV for which funds be located in consultation with Ministry of 
Finance and the Planning Commission.  It is  considered that si nce these projects are 
non-viable, funding through SPV mechanism may not be amenable.  Considering this, 
the proposal is under process for reconsideration of the Government.” 
 

 9 
 
1.7 The committee are satisfied to note that in order to expedite the 
completion of projects Railways ha ve taken various initiatives including 
transfer of doublings and othe r throughput enhancement works  to Rail 
Vikas Nigam Limited.  The Committee hope that these measures will enable 
the Railways  to achieve the desired targets.  However, the Committee are 
not satisfied with the progress of Bogibeel Mega Bridge and Rangia-
Murkong Selek (Gauge Conversion) projects.  They reiterate their earlier 
recommendation that these projects be declared as National Projects at the 
earliest and completed within a given time frame.

the Planning Commission with  an outlay of Rs. 60,600 crore comprising Rs. 27,600

Market Borrowings.  The object ives of the Plan were inter- alia to strengthen the high 
density network, build up capacity through National Rail Vikas Yojana, upgrade 
technological assets for improving effici ency, improve safety of operations by 
replacement of over aged assets, utilizatio n of information te chnology for better 
customer interface and complete sanctioned ra il projects.   However, they find that in 
the terminal  year i.e. 2006-07 the financial targets of the Plan are likely to be Rs.

 As against this phenomenal increase  in financial outlay the physical

Plan Heads Track Renewals, Gauge Conversion and Rolling Stocks.  The targets fixed
